## Continuous-time Markov chains and jump processes — Day 2, Session 1

Worksheet: `worksheets/05-continuous-time-markov-chains-and-jump-processes.qmd`. The chapter is
[Continuous-time Markov chains and jump
processes](../chapters/05-jump-processes.qmd).

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-setup
using ModelingToolkit
using JumpProcesses
using CairoMakie
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

# An earlier part of this appendix binds `t` to a vector of solution times, so
# take the symbolic time variable by assignment rather than by import.
t = ModelingToolkit.t_nounits

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

@parameters κ σ γ
@variables S(t) E(t) I(t) R(t)

κ_value = 0.05 * 10 / 1000   # β c / N
σ_value = 0.5                # mean latent period 1/σ = 2 days
γ_value = 0.25
grid = 0.0:0.5:120.0
tspan = (0.0, last(grid))

println("R₀ = ", 0.05 * 10 / γ_value)
```

### Part A — an exposed compartment

The two gaps are about keeping the `MassActionJump` lists apart: the reactant
list sets the propensity, the net list says what the event does. Infection needs
`I` present, and an exposed person becomes infectious rather than recovered.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-a1
infection = MassActionJump(κ,
    [S => 1, I => 1],                        # infection needs two people
    [S => -1, E => 1];
    scale_rates = false)

progression = MassActionJump(σ,
    [E => 1],
    [E => -1, I => 1];                       # an exposed person becomes infectious
    scale_rates = false)

recovery = MassActionJump(γ,
    [I => 1],
    [I => -1, R => 1];
    scale_rates = false)

@named seir = JumpSystem([infection, progression, recovery], t,
                         [S, E, I, R], [κ, σ, γ])
seir_system = complete(seir)

seir_start = [S => 990, E => 0, I => 10, R => 0,
              κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]

seir_problem(seed; start = seir_start) =
    JumpProblem(seir_system, start, tspan; rng = StableRNG(seed))

solution = solve(seir_problem(1), SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)

# With nobody infectious, a correct propensity makes every event impossible.
quiet = solve(seir_problem(2; start = [S => 1000, E => 0, I => 0, R => 0,
                                       κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]),
              SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)

check("population conserved",
      all(solution[S] .+ solution[E] .+ solution[I] .+ solution[R] .== 1000))
check("infection needs an infectious person present", all(quiet[S] .== 1000))
check("exposed individuals go on to become infectious", maximum(solution[I]) > 10)
println("peak infectious = ", maximum(solution[I]),
        ", ever infected = ", solution[R][end])
```

#### A1. Interpret

- Infection requires a meeting between two people, so its propensity is
  proportional to the product $SI$ and falls to zero if either compartment
  empties. Progression and recovery are things an individual does on their own
  schedule, so each is proportional to the single compartment it drains.
- `I` belongs in the reactant list because it must be *present*, and not in the
  net list because an infectious person is unchanged by infecting someone.
- Moving `I` between the lists breaks the model twice over: the propensity would
  become $\kappa S$, so infections would fire with nobody infectious present, and
  the event would create an infectious person directly, bypassing the latent
  period. The `quiet` run is what catches the first error — without it the curve
  still looks roughly right.
- Conservation is exact here for a structural reason rather than a numerical one.
  Each net list sums to zero, so the total is invariant by construction, which is
  why the check can use `==` rather than `isapprox`.
- The state is read symbolically, `solution[I]`, rather than by row number. The
  SIR system built in Part B has different unknowns, so the same compartment sits
  in a different row; asking by name cannot pick up the wrong one.

### Part B — does the latent period matter?

`prob_func` is the piece worth pausing on: it gives trajectory `ctx.sim_id` its
own seed. Without it every trajectory would share one random stream, which is a
correctness problem once the runs are threaded.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-b1
seir_ensemble = EnsembleProblem(seir_problem(100);
    prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> seir_problem(100 + ctx.sim_id))

seir_runs = solve(seir_ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads();
                  trajectories = 30, saveat = grid)

peaks = [maximum(r[I]) for r in seir_runs.u]

check("the runs differ from each other", std(peaks) > 0)
println("peak infectious over 30 runs: mean ", round(mean(peaks); digits = 1),
        ", sd ", round(std(peaks); digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-b2
sir_start = [S => 990, I => 10, R => 0, κ => κ_value, γ => γ_value]

@named sir = JumpSystem(
    [MassActionJump(κ, [S => 1, I => 1], [S => -1, I => 1]; scale_rates = false),
     MassActionJump(γ, [I => 1], [I => -1, R => 1]; scale_rates = false)],
    t, [S, I, R], [κ, γ])
sir_system = complete(sir)

sir_problem(seed) = JumpProblem(sir_system, sir_start, tspan; rng = StableRNG(seed))

function summarise(make_problem, seed0; trajectories = 30)
    ensemble = EnsembleProblem(make_problem(seed0);
                               prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> make_problem(seed0 + ctx.sim_id))
    runs = solve(ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads();
                 trajectories = trajectories, saveat = grid)
    return EnsembleSummary(runs, grid)
end

seir_summary = summarise(seir_problem, 100)
sir_summary = summarise(sir_problem, 200)

# Row order follows the unknowns, so I is row 3 for SEIR and row 2 for SIR.
seir_mean = reduce(hcat, seir_summary.u.u)
sir_mean = reduce(hcat, sir_summary.u.u)
seir_I, sir_I = seir_mean[3, :], sir_mean[2, :]
seir_final, sir_final = seir_mean[4, end], sir_mean[3, end]

check("the SEIR peak comes later", grid[argmax(seir_I)] > grid[argmax(sir_I)])
check("the SEIR peak is lower", maximum(seir_I) < maximum(sir_I))
check("both reach a similar final size",
      abs(seir_final - sir_final) / sir_final < 0.05)
(; seir_peak_day = grid[argmax(seir_I)], sir_peak_day = grid[argmax(sir_I)],
   seir_peak = round(maximum(seir_I); digits = 1),
   sir_peak = round(maximum(sir_I); digits = 1),
   seir_final = round(seir_final; digits = 1),
   sir_final = round(sir_final; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch05-compare
#| fig-cap: "Mean infectious curve over 30 exact simulations, with and without a latent period, with the 5th-95th percentile band for the SEIR model (the `EnsembleSummary` default)."
seir_low = reduce(hcat, seir_summary.qlow.u)[3, :]
seir_high = reduce(hcat, seir_summary.qhigh.u)[3, :]

fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "mean infectious")
band!(ax, grid, seir_low, seir_high; color = (:steelblue, 0.2))
lines!(ax, grid, sir_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "SIR")
lines!(ax, grid, seir_I; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "SEIR")
xlims!(ax, 0, 70)
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

#### B1. Interpret

- The SEIR mean peaks at 95.4 on day 31, against 146.6 on day 18.5 for SIR:
  about a third lower and nearly two weeks later. Both end with approximately the
  same number ever infected, 793.0 and 802.2.
- The two "peak" numbers in this part are different quantities. The ensemble
  reports a mean of each run's *own* maximum, 111.7 with a standard deviation of
  11.7, while the comparison takes the maximum of the *averaged* curve, 95.4. The
  first is always the larger, because individual peaks fall on different days and
  averaging the curves flattens them.
- Adding $E$ does not change how many people each infectious person infects, so
  $R_0 = \beta c/\gamma = 2$ and the final size are unchanged. Read that
  narrowly: for this model and a fixed initial state the deterministic final-size
  relation involves $R_0$ and nothing about the latent period.
- What changes is the clock. Every infection now waits an average of two extra
  days before it can transmit, so the same total number of infections is spread
  over more time and fewer of them overlap. Prevalence counts overlap, so the
  peak falls.
- Two outbreaks with identical $R_0$ and identical final size can place very
  different demands on a health system, because the peak is what decides whether
  capacity is exceeded.
- The band is narrow at the start because every run begins in the same state, and
  widest near the peak because runs identical in shape but a few days apart in
  timing are far apart in *level* there. It reports spread in timing more than
  spread in severity.

#### B2. Experiment

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-b3
latent_rates = [1.0, 0.5, 0.25]

for s in latent_rates
    start = [S => 990, E => 0, I => 10, R => 0,
             κ => κ_value, σ => s, γ => γ_value]
    summary = summarise(seed -> seir_problem(seed; start = start), 300;
                        trajectories = 10)
    mean_I = reduce(hcat, summary.u.u)[3, :]
    println("mean latent period ", round(1 / s; digits = 1), " days → peak on day ",
            grid[argmax(mean_I)])
end

check("three latent periods tried", length(latent_rates) == 3)
```

- Peaks land on day 24.5, day 30.5 and day 45.0 for mean latent periods of 1, 2
  and 4 days.
- Lengthening the latent period pushes the peak later, and faster than
  one-for-one: adding two days moved the peak by about 15, because the delay
  applies once per generation of infection and compounds over successive
  generations.
- $R_0$ is unchanged throughout. None of these runs alters how many people a case
  infects, only how long it takes.

### Part C — how often does an outbreak fizzle out?

The only change is the starting state: one infectious individual means 999
susceptible ones.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-c1
single_case = [S => 999, E => 0, I => 1, R => 0,
               κ => κ_value, σ => σ_value, γ => γ_value]

# Outcomes are bimodal — a handful of cases, or hundreds — so the cut at 20 is
# not a delicate choice.
fade_ensemble = EnsembleProblem(
    seir_problem(5000; start = single_case);
    prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> seir_problem(5000 + ctx.sim_id; start = single_case),
    output_func = (sol, ctx) -> (sol[R][end] < 20, false))

trials = 400
faded = solve(fade_ensemble, SSAStepper(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories = trials)
fade_fraction = count(faded.u) / trials
predicted = γ_value / (0.05 * 10)   # 1 / R₀

check("fade-out is close to the branching prediction",
      abs(fade_fraction - predicted) < 0.05)
(; fade_fraction, predicted)
```

#### C1. Interpret

- The 400 trials give a fade-out fraction of 0.4825, against a prediction of
  $1/R_0 = 0.5$.
- While cases are few each infectious individual behaves independently of the
  others, so the early stage is a linear birth–death process. Because infectious
  lifetimes are exponential here, its extinction probability from one initial
  case is $q = \gamma/(\beta c) = 1/R_0$ when $R_0 > 1$. The formula belongs to
  that approximation and is not universal across offspring or infectious-period
  distributions.
- The latent period does not change it, because every exposed person eventually
  progresses to $I$.
- Two approximations separate the argument from the measurement, and both are
  small here rather than zero: the branching process never depletes its
  susceptible pool, while this one has 999 susceptibles, and "died out" was
  scored as fewer than 20 ever infected. Running 20,000 trials gives 0.4974
  against 0.500, so the gap at 400 trials is mostly sampling noise.
- The threshold is not delicate either. Cutting at 10, 20, 50 or 100 ever
  infected gives 0.4866, 0.4974, 0.4992 and 0.4992 over those 20,000 trials.
  Cutting at 2 gives 0.3329, which asks a different question — whether the index
  case infected anyone at all.
- The deterministic model cannot produce this answer. It has neither random event
  counts nor the absorbing state $E = I = 0$, so from $I(0) = 1$ it produces the
  same non-extinguishing trajectory every time. Nor is it the finite-population
  average: an ensemble mean can fall between the fade-out and major-outbreak
  branches and resemble neither.
- Starting from 10 infectious individuals, as Parts A and B do, fade-out has
  probability $(1/R_0)^{10} \approx 0.001$, which is why it was never seen there.
